Sunday afternoon. Ludwig, still with the cast on his hand, gives Mara her weekly German lesson in exchange for the phone lesson. Today's topic: childhood.
Right, Mara, today we're talking about childhood. Where did you grow up?
In Sibiu, in an old house with a garden. In summer I was always at my grandparents' in the countryside, in Rășinari.
And what did you want to be when you were a child?
At first I wanted to be a vet. Then a singer. At fourteen I wanted to become a nurse, like my aunt.
And your parents? Were they strict?
My dad wasn't, my mum was. I had to study for two hours every day and I was only allowed to go out after my homework.
Two hours! I had to help my father in the workshop after school. He had a small bicycle workshop.
At weekends were you allowed to do what you wanted?
On Sundays, yes. Then I could play with my friends on the ruins. Berlin was still full of ruins from the war back then.
On the ruins? Wasn't it dangerous?
Of course! We weren't supposed to play there. My mother strictly forbade it. But we were children. We wanted adventures!
And did you always want to be a tram driver?
No! I wanted to be a guitarist, like Elvis. But in the GDR you couldn't just become a rock star. So I became a tram driver. And you know what? I don't regret a thing.

No umlaut in the past: konnte = “KON-teh” (not “KÖN-teh”), musste = “MOOS-teh”.
For modal verbs, Germans almost always use the Präteritum (not the Perfekt) for the past. It's formed from the stem WITHOUT umlaut + -te:
The umlaut disappears: können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte. “mögen” becomes “mochte” (with “ch”).
As in the present: ich and er have the same form, with no extra ending: ich konnte, er konnte.
2. The word order stays the same
The modal in the past still goes in position 2, and the infinitive still goes at the end:
I had to study for two hours every day.
As a child I wasn't allowed to go into town on my own.
Watch the difference in meaning: “Ich sollte lernen” = I was supposed to study (others asked me to). “Ich musste lernen” = I was obliged to. And “ich sollte” can also mean “I should” (chap. 24).
Perfekt: “ist geworden” (with SEIN, it's a change of state): “Er ist Straßenbahnfahrer geworden.”

It's Wednesday, Mara's day on the fourth floor. Mrs Hoffmann has made tea, black tea with lemon, in fine old cups with blue flowers. It's raining outside. Mara takes her blood pressure: a hundred and forty over ninety. Not perfect, but good for ninety.
On the piano there's a small black-and-white photo: a girl of about eight, with plaits, in front of a destroyed house. Mara has seen it many times. Today she asks.
Mrs Hoffmann, is that you in the photo?
Yes, child. That's me, in the summer of 1945. The house behind me was our house. Here in Prenzlauer Berg, two streets from here. After the war it was just a ruin.
Mrs Hoffmann puts down her cup and looks out of the window, into the rain. Then she tells her story, slowly, as if she were taking the words out of a deep drawer.

I was born in 1936. When the war started, I was three. I don't remember much, only the nights in the cellar. When the bombs came, we all had to run down to the cellar, the whole family and all the neighbours. We weren't allowed to take anything, only a small bag.

There was an old piano in the cellar. Nobody knew whose it was. It was out of tune, and three keys were broken. But on the long nights I was allowed to play it. My mother used to say: “Play, Grete. That way we don't hear the bombs so loudly.”
Could you already play back then?

No, not at all! I couldn't read music. I just played whatever was in my head. Children's songs, Christmas carols, tunes from the radio. The neighbours sang along with me. An old man, Mr Lewin, always cried when I played “Good moon, you go so quietly”.

In April 1945, the house was hit. We were in the cellar and we survived. But the piano was gone, under the stones. I cried for days. My mother couldn't understand it. We had no home, no food, no father, and I was crying over a broken piano.

Mara listens and says nothing. She thinks about her own childhood: her biggest worry back then was a bad mark in maths. She never had to run into a cellar. She could go to her grandparents' every summer.

He was a soldier. He came back from captivity in 1948, very thin, very quiet. He never talked about the war. Never. But he had an idea. He sold his gold watch on the black market and paid for piano lessons for me. With an old teacher on Schönhauser Allee. She was very strict. I had to practise three hours every day. In summer I wasn't allowed to go swimming, because of my hands.
Did you sometimes want to give up?
Every day! I wanted to play with the other children, on the ruins, like your Ludwig. But I had to become a pianist. That was my father's dream. And at some point it became my dream too.
Mara looks at the photo, then at Mrs Hoffmann's old hands. They're thin and covered in spots, but the fingers are still long and straight.
At twenty I gave my first concert, at the Konzerthaus. My father sat in the front row, in his only suit. He didn't cry. He just smiled, the whole time. A year later he died.
The room is silent. Only the rain beats against the windows. Then Mrs Hoffmann gets up, very slowly, with her hand on Mara's shoulder, and sits down at the piano.
You know what, child? I'll play you the song for Mr Lewin. I haven't played it for years.

It's a simple song, a children's song, just a few notes. But Mara thinks of her grandmother in Rășinari, of the house with the garden, of the summer evenings when she was little, didn't have to do anything and was allowed to do everything. And only at the end does she realise she's crying.

On the stairs she meets Ludwig, who's coming back from a walk with Fritz. He sees her eyes and doesn't ask anything. He just says: “Margarete played, didn't she? The song about the moon.” Mara nods. Ludwig nods too. “She used to play it for the whole street”, he says. “In summer, with the window open. When I was a child.”
